definition: Computer vision tasks include methods for acquiring, processing, analyzing, and understanding digital images, and extraction of high-dimensional data from the real world in order to produce numerical or symbolic information, e.g.
details: in the form of decisions. "Understanding" in this context signifies the transformation of visual images into descriptions of the world that make sense to thought processes and can elicit appropriate action. This image understanding can be seen as the disentangling of symbolic information from image data using models constructed with the aid of geometry, physics, statistics, and learning theory. The scientific discipline of computer vision is concerned with the theory behind artificial systems that extract information from images. Image data can take many forms, such as video sequences, views from multiple cameras, multi-dimensional data from a 3D scanner, 3D point clouds from LiDaR sensors, or medical scanning devices. The technological discipline of computer vision seeks to apply its theories and models to the construction of computer vision systems. Subdisciplines of computer vision include scene reconstruction, object detection, event detection, activity recognition, video tracking, object recognition, 3D pose estimation, learning, indexing, motion estimation, visual servoing, 3D scene modeling, and image restoration.

explainer.lead: Computer vision gives artificial systems a way to turn images and other visual measurements into useful descriptions of the world. Those descriptions can support decisions and actions, from recognizing objects to reconstructing a 3D scene.

tiers.eli5: Computer vision is like teaching a computer to make sense of what a camera sees. Instead of treating a picture as just colored dots, the computer works out useful information, such as where an object is or how something is moving. That information can then help a machine decide what to do.
tiers.practitioner: Engineers apply computer vision to video, multi-camera views, 3D scanner data, LiDaR point clouds, and medical scans. A system may combine geometry, physics, statistics, and learning theory to produce detections, tracks, poses, motion estimates, or reconstructed scenes. The input representation and output must fit the intended task, especially when the result drives visual servoing or another action.
tiers.paperLevel: Let I denote image data, which may include video, multiple views, or multi-dimensional sensor measurements. Computer vision constructs a model f, using geometry, physics, statistics, and learning theory, such that f(I) = y, where y is numerical or symbolic information such as objects, activities, motion, or 3D structure; a subsequent decision or action can be expressed as a = g(y). The discipline covers both the theory of this information extraction and the construction of working systems.

explainer.example: A system receives views from several cameras and tracks an object through the video sequence. It estimates the object's motion and 3D pose, turning the images into numerical information that another system can use to choose an appropriate action.

explainer.intuition: An image contains measurements, but people and machines need meaningful descriptions. Computer vision bridges that gap by disentangling symbolic information from visual data so a system can understand a scene and respond appropriately.
howItWorks: Acquire visual data from images, video, multiple cameras, or sensing devices.
Process the data into a form suitable for analysis.
Apply models based on geometry, physics, statistics, or learning theory.
Extract numerical or symbolic descriptions such as objects, motion, poses, or scene structure.
Use those descriptions to produce a decision or action.
explainer.whyItMatters: It connects raw visual measurements with decisions and actions. The same underlying discipline supports tasks ranging from image restoration and object recognition to activity recognition and 3D scene modeling.
misconceptions: Computer vision is not limited to ordinary photographs; its inputs can include video, multiple views, 3D scans, LiDaR point clouds, and medical scans.
Recognizing objects is only one task, alongside reconstruction, tracking, motion estimation, restoration, and others.
Image understanding means producing descriptions that support reasoning or action, not merely storing or displaying pixels.
